Probably not yet — you likely need a plan, not an advisor.
• Cost: 1% of assets yearly is enormous over decades.
• DIY: index funds + a target-date fund need no advisor.
• Worth it when: you're near retirement, have complex taxes, or a windfall.
• Alternative: a one-time fee-only planner ($200-400/hr) for a checkup.
Do the fee-only checkup every few years. Skip the 1%-forever advisor until you're wealthy.

input: should I buy a condo or a house
muse_response:
House, if you can afford it — condo if that's what the budget allows.
• Appreciation: houses (with land) appreciate better long-term.
• HOA: condo fees rise and you can't control them.
• Maintenance: condos cover exterior — less work for you.
• Lifestyle: condos suit low-maintenance living; houses suit space needs.
Buy the house if the payment works. Buy the condo if it gets you in the market years earlier.

input: should i switch banks
muse_response:
Yes, if your bank charges you fees.
• Fees: monthly maintenance and overdraft fees are a tax on loyalty.
• Switch to: a no-fee online bank or credit union.
• Effort: switching takes about an hour — direct deposits and autopays.
• Keep: the old account open a month to catch stragglers.
If you're paying any monthly fee, switch this weekend. It's an hour of work for hundreds a year.

input: should I take a gap year
muse_response:
Yes, if you have a plan for it.
• Good gap year: working, traveling with purpose, or building skills.
• Bad gap year: drifting at home for 12 months.
• College: most schools let you defer admission — ask.
• Maturity: a purposeful year makes you a better student after.
Take it if you can name what you'll do each quarter. Don't take it to 'figure things out' with no structure.

input: should i buy stocks or index funds
muse_response:
Index funds, for 95% of people.
• Diversification: one fund holds thousands of companies.
• Time: stock-picking is a part-time job; index funds are set-and-forget.
• Returns: most professional fund managers lose to index funds.
• Fun money: keep 5% for individual stocks if you enjoy it.
Put 95% in a total-market index fund. Play with 5% if stock-picking entertains you.

input: should I get a pet cat or dog
muse_response:
Cat, if you want lower maintenance. Dog, if you want a companion.
• Time: dogs need 1-2 hours daily; cats need 20 minutes.
• Space: cats thrive in apartments; dogs need room and walks.
• Cost: cats are cheaper — roughly half the yearly cost.
• Bonding: dogs bond harder; cats bond on their terms.
Busy life or apartment: cat. Active lifestyle with time: dog. Both are 15-year commitments.

input: should i doordash as a side gig
muse_response:
Yes, as a short-term cash bridge — not a career.
• Pay: $15-22/hour realistically after gas and wear.
• Flexibility: the real perk — work whenever.
• Car costs: track mileage; the IRS deduction matters at tax time.
• Better: use it for 3 months to build savings, then pivot.
Good for quick cash and flexible hours. Bad as a long-term plan — your car depreciates faster than you earn.

input: should I buy the warranty on a used car
muse_response:
Usually no — buy a reliable car instead.
• Math: third-party warranties are priced to profit, with lots of exclusions.
• Read: the fine print excludes exactly what breaks most.
• Better: get a pre-purchase inspection ($150) and buy a Toyota/Honda.
• Exception: certified pre-owned manufacturer warranties are actually decent.
Skip the third-party warranty. Spend the money on the inspection and a reliable brand.

input: should i get lasik
muse_response:
Yes, if you're a good candidate and hate glasses/contacts.
• Candidacy: stable prescription for 2+ years and thick enough corneas — the exam decides.
• Cost: $2,000-4,000 total; breaks even vs contacts in ~5 years.
• Risk: dry eyes are the most common side effect; serious complications are rare.
• Age: best in your 20s-30s before presbyopia hits.
Get the consultation — it's usually free. If you're a candidate, it's life-changing for most people.

input: should I move in with my partner
muse_response:
Yes, if the relationship is solid — but protect yourself.
• Money: split costs fairly and keep a joint spreadsheet from day one.
• Exit plan: agree beforehand what happens to the lease if you split.
• Trial: it's the best compatibility test that exists.
• Timing: move in because you want to, not to save rent.
Do it for the relationship, not the rent savings. Write down the money rules before the boxes arrive.

input: should i buy a treadmill
muse_response:
Only if you'll use it 3+ times a week.
• Reality: most home treadmills become clothing racks within 6 months.
• Space: they dominate a room — measure first.
• Cost: decent ones start at $800; cheap ones break.
• Test: run outside or at a gym consistently for a month first.
Prove the habit before buying the machine. If you've run 3x/week for a month, buy it.

input: should I get a Costco executive membership
muse_response:
Yes, if you spend $250+/month at Costco.
• Math: 2% back on $3,000/year = $60, covering the $60 upgrade.
• Risk: none — they refund the difference if you don't earn it back.
• Stack: pair with the Costco credit card for another 2%.
• Track: check your annual reward before renewing.
It's free money if you shop there regularly — and refundable if the math doesn't work.

input: should i learn spanish or french
muse_response:
Spanish, for most Americans.
• Usefulness: 40+ million US speakers — you'll actually use it.
• Travel: all of Latin America plus Spain.
• Difficulty: Spanish pronunciation is more consistent for English speakers.
• French wins if: you're moving to France/Quebec or love the culture.
Learn the language you'll speak. For most people in the US, that's Spanish.

input: should I buy an iPad for my kid
muse_response:
Only with strict boundaries set first.
• Learning: great for reading apps and creative tools.
• Zombie risk: unlimited YouTube Kids is not educational — set limits before handing it over.
• Setup: use Screen Time to lock it down on day one.
• Age: under 5, skip it; 6+ with limits is reasonable.
Buy it, but configure parental controls before the kid ever touches it. The setup matters more than the device.

input: is a home warranty worth it
muse_response:
Usually no — they're profit machines.
• Coverage: the fine print excludes most of what actually breaks.
• Claims: denied claims are the #1 complaint.
• Better: put the $500/year premium in a home repair fund.
• Exception: useful for first-time buyers nervous about surprise costs, for year one only.
Skip it and self-insure. If you must, buy one year max while you learn the house.

input: is pet insurance worth it
muse_response:
Yes, for puppies, kittens, and accident-prone breeds.
• Emergencies: one surgery can cost $5,000-10,000.
• Math: $30-60/month vs one catastrophic bill.
• Get it early: pre-existing conditions aren't covered — enroll while they're healthy.
• Skip if: you have $10k in savings you'd happily spend on the pet.
Enroll in the first year. It's the one insurance that's emotionally easy to justify.

input: is a VPN worth it
muse_response:
For public wifi and privacy, yes. For 'security,' it's oversold.
• Public wifi: a VPN genuinely protects you on coffee-shop networks.
• Privacy: hides browsing from your ISP, not from Google or Facebook.
• Streaming: useful for accessing other countries' libraries.
• Cost: $3-5/month for a reputable one; free VPNs sell your data.
Worth it if you work from cafes or travel. Skip if you're always on trusted home wifi.

input: is hiring a cleaning service worth it
muse_response:
Yes, if your hourly rate beats theirs.
• Math: 3 hours of cleaning at $150 vs 3 hours of your time — what's your time worth?
• Sanity: coming home to a clean house is a real quality-of-life upgrade.
• Frequency: biweekly is the sweet spot for most homes.
• Trial: book one deep clean and see how you feel.
If you earn more per hour than the cleaner costs, it's irrational not to outsource it.

input: is grad school worth the debt
muse_response:
Only if the salary bump pays the debt in under 5 years.
• Math: $100k debt needs ~$25k/year in extra salary to make sense.
• Funded programs: PhDs and some master's are free — those are always worth considering.
• Employer-paid: changes everything; do it.
• Prestige debt: the most expensive mistake — the name fades, the loans don't.
Run the numbers for your specific field. If the payback is over 7 years, it's a no.
